best_for: Windows PC owners who still manage a local music library, burn CDs or keep audiobooks and podcasts in one place, and who have not moved to Apple's newer Windows apps.
description:
iTunes is Apple's media player and store app for Windows PCs. It plays and organizes your music and video, and it opens the iTunes Store, where you can buy, rent or pre-order items, send them as gifts and keep a wish list.

You can import songs from your CDs with the import settings you choose, or bring in music from other computers on your network through Home Sharing. You can make standard playlists and Smart Playlists, group them in folders, and save a copy of your playlists. The MiniPlayer keeps playback controls in a small window while you work, and you can listen to internet radio. iTunes can also back up an iPhone or iPad, and with the iTunes Remote app you control playback from your phone.

points.title: Apple split it into three apps
points.text: On Windows, Apple now offers Apple Music, Apple TV and Apple Devices from the Microsoft Store. Apple Devices handles syncing iPhones and iPads.

points.title: What iTunes keeps once they are installed
points.text: After you install the new apps, Apple says iTunes remains the home for audiobooks and free podcasts. Without them, iTunes still handles all your media.

points.title: Windows only, Mac moved on
points.text: iTunes is a Windows download now. On a current Mac the same jobs belong to Music, TV, Podcasts and Books.

points.title: Modest requirements
points.text: Apple lists Windows 10, 400 MB of disk, a 1 GHz processor with SSE2 and 512 MB of RAM. HD video wants more: 2 GB of RAM and a 2.4 GHz Core 2 Duo for 1080p.

points.title: Free app, paid content
points.text: iTunes is free. Apple Music needs a subscription, and songs from Apple Music cannot be burned to CD.

points.title: Pick the right bitness
points.text: 64-bit Windows needs the 64-bit installer. This page lists both 32-bit and 64-bit builds, which install for all users, and keeps 26 Windows versions.
